glossary.Herpesvirus: A family of DNA viruses that stay in the body for life after first infection, including VZV and herpes simplex.
glossary.Double-stranded DNA: Genetic material made of two paired strands; herpesviruses carry their genome this way.
glossary.Reactivation: When a virus that has lain dormant in the body starts replicating again and causes disease.
glossary.Primary infection: The first time a person is infected with a particular organism.
glossary.Immunosuppressed: Having a weakened immune system, for example from chemotherapy, steroids, HIV or transplant drugs.
glossary.Crusts: Dried scabs that form as blisters break and heal; once all lesions crust, chickenpox is no longer infectious.
glossary.Unilateral: On one side of the body only.
glossary.Secondary bacterial infection: A bacterial infection that takes hold on top of an existing illness, such as infected chickenpox spots.
glossary.Low birth weight: A baby weighing under 2.5 kg at birth.
glossary.Skin scarring: Permanent marks left in the skin after damage heals.
glossary.Vesicle fluid: Clear fluid inside a blister; in VZV it is full of virus and can be swabbed for PCR.
glossary.Immunity: Protection against an infection, from past infection or vaccination, shown by IgG antibodies.
glossary.Non-immune: Having no protective antibodies against an infection, so able to catch it.
glossary.Neuropathic pain: Pain caused by damage to nerves themselves, often burning, shooting or electric.
glossary.Antidepressants: Drugs for depression; some, like amitriptyline and duloxetine, also dampen nerve pain.
glossary.Ibuprofen: A common NSAID painkiller; avoided in chickenpox because of necrotising fasciitis risk.
glossary.Paracetamol: A simple painkiller and fever reducer, safe in chickenpox.
glossary.IV: Intravenous: given directly into a vein.
glossary.Shingles vaccine: A vaccine that boosts immunity to VZV to cut the risk of shingles; offered in the UK at age 65.
glossary.Respiratory droplets: Small drops from coughs and sneezes that carry infection between people.
glossary.Transplacental: Passing across the placenta from mother to fetus.
glossary.Limb buds: The early swellings in the embryo that grow into arms and legs.
glossary.Fetus: The developing baby in the womb from about 8 weeks until birth.
glossary.Sensory nerve: A nerve that carries feeling (touch, pain, temperature) from the skin to the spinal cord.
glossary.Inflammation: The body's response to injury or infection, with swelling, redness, heat and pain.
glossary.Immunocompromised: Having a weakened immune system that copes poorly with infections.
glossary.Ganglia: Clusters of nerve cell bodies outside the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.NICE CKS: NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries: short UK guidance on managing common conditions in primary care.
glossary.RCOG: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, which writes UK pregnancy guidelines.
glossary.Green-top Guideline: An evidence-based clinical guideline published by the RCOG.
glossary.Antiviral: A drug that stops a virus replicating, such as aciclovir.
